name: Polygenic Risk Scores
title: Polygenic Risk Scores
answer: Polygenic risk scores summarize the combined effect of many common genetic variants on a trait or disease. They are used in genomic medicine to estimate inherited susceptibility for conditions such as coronary artery disease, type 2 diabetes, breast cancer, and prostate cancer. A score is not a diagnosis and does not capture rare variants, family history, or environmental exposures. The scope also includes research on trait prediction, risk stratification, and screening enrichment.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Polygenic risk scores summarize the combined effect of many common genetic variants on a trait or disease. They are used in genomic medicine to estimate inherited susceptibility for conditions such as coronary artery disease, type 2 diabetes, breast cancer, and prostate cancer. A score is not a diagnosis and does not capture rare variants, family history, or environmental exposures. The scope also includes research on trait prediction, risk stratification, and screening enrichment.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Polygenic risk score pipelines run on genotype array data, whole genome or exome sequencing, and imputed genotypes from reference panels such as the 1000 Genomes Project or UK Biobank. They depend on genome-wide association study summary statistics, linkage disequilibrium reference panels, and large biobank cohorts for training and validation. Computation ranges from CPU-based regression and clumping to GPU-accelerated Bayesian methods and cloud workflows. Standard tools include PLINK, LDpred, PRS-CS, and PRSice.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins with quality control of genotype data, imputation, and selection of variants from genome-wide association study summary statistics. Analysts then apply methods such as clumping and thresholding, penalized regression, or Bayesian shrinkage to estimate weights, often adjusting for linkage disequilibrium. Scores are validated in independent cohorts, calibrated for the target population, and compared with existing clinical risk models. Ancestry adjustment and multi-ancestry training are increasingly part of the workflow because portability across populations is limited.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Provenance covers consent for biobank and cohort data, data access agreements, and the source of genome-wide association study summary statistics. Risks include re-identification from genotype data, misestimation of risk in underrepresented ancestries, and potential insurance or employment discrimination. Governance also involves return of results, clinical validation, and transparency about score limitations. The site's 215 compliance and regulation pages track the wider rules that shape this work.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Research is moving toward multi-ancestry scores, integration with electronic health records, and combination with monogenic and clinical risk factors. Pharmacogenomic and disease-specific scores are being tested in prospective studies and learning health systems. Regulatory and ethical frameworks are developing for clinical use, including standards for analytical validity and clinical utility. The field is also exploring how polygenic risk scores can inform screening and prevention without widening health disparities.
